note: Facts for 'The Labyrinth' (Pac-Man): the soul's passage through the maze of the dead. Re-sourced (D1) to ch47 'Journeys to the Underworld', the comparative chapter the game is themed on. Each fact's `basis` substring must appear in ch47's rendered text (tools/verify-pacman.js).

facts.label: The seven gates
facts.fact: In the oldest descent we can read, Inanna goes down to her sister Ereshkigal, surrendering one mark of power at each of the underworld's seven gates until she arrives naked and bowed low.

facts.label: The land of no return
facts.fact: The Mesopotamian dead went to a bleak 'land of no return' — a house whose dwellers are deprived of light, where dust is their food and clay their bread.

facts.label: Katabasis
facts.fact: The Greeks named the journey katabasis, the 'going down' — and, almost uniquely, their heroes went into Hades and came back.

facts.label: The ferryman Charon
facts.fact: Aeneas made the fullest journey of all, guided by the Sibyl past the ferryman Charon and the rivers of the dead.

facts.label: The Duat
facts.fact: The Egyptian dead travelled through the Duat, the underworld through which the sun-god himself sailed each night, battling the serpent Apophis before rising reborn at dawn.

facts.label: The weighing of the heart
facts.fact: The climax of the Book of the Dead is the Weighing of the Heart, set on a balance against the feather of Maat — death imagined, earlier than anywhere, as a moral reckoning.

facts.label: Ammit the Devourer
facts.fact: If the heart is heavy with wrongdoing it is thrown to Ammit, 'the Devourer' — part crocodile, part lion, part hippopotamus — and the soul is annihilated.

facts.label: The Chinvat bridge
facts.fact: Zoroastrianism sends every soul across the Chinvat bridge, which widens for the righteous and narrows to a knife-edge for the wicked — one of the earliest clear afterlife judgments.

facts.label: The bureaucratic hell
facts.fact: Chinese religion built a vast bureaucratic underworld, Diyu, with courts, magistrates, and registers administering karmic punishment — the afterlife imagined as an imperial government.

facts.label: The un-judged dead
facts.fact: Not every underworld weighed its dead: the Norse Hel was, for the most part, simply where you went if you did not die in battle — no divine tribunal decided it.
